n: The last of the Passover Hallel psalms — likely the hymn Jesus sang with his disciples before Gethsemane. It begins and ends with the same call to thanksgiving.
A responsive call: let all Israel declare that God’s covenant love lasts forever.
Let the priests, Aaron’s family, say it too.
And let all who revere the Lord join in — the same three groups as Psalm 115.

f.w: them now that fear the LORD

n: In a tight spot he called to God, and God answered by setting him in a ‘large place’ — wide open freedom.

f.g: Open space; freedom from being hemmed in.

n: With the Lord on his side, he has nothing to fear from any human. Hebrews quotes this verse.

f.w: what can man do unto me?

n: The Lord is among his helpers, so he will see his enemies defeated.

f.g: Is on my side, among my helpers.

n: Trusting God is better than relying on people. Some have noted this verse sits near the middle of the Bible’s verses.

f.w: better to trust in the LORD

n: Even powerful rulers are less reliable than God.
The speaker — perhaps a king leading worship — recalls being surrounded by hostile nations, yet driving them off in the Lord’s name.

f.w: in the name of the LORD

n: The repetition of ‘compassed me about’ makes us feel the enemies closing in.
They swarmed like angry bees, but burned out as quickly as a fire of thorns.

f.g: Dry thorns blaze up fast and die out fast.

n: The enemy pushed hard to make him fall, but the Lord helped him.
These words come from the Song of Moses at the Red Sea: the Lord is my strength, my song, and my salvation.

f.w: The LORD is my strength and song

n: Shouts of joy and victory ring out from the tents of the righteous: the Lord’s right hand acts mightily.
The triple praise of God’s ‘right hand’ — his power — builds to a climax.

f.w: The right hand of the LORD is exalted

n: ‘I will not die but live, and tell what the Lord has done.’ Christians hear in this the victory of the risen Christ.

f.w: I shall not die, but live

n: The Lord disciplined him severely but did not let him die. Hardship refined him rather than destroyed him.
Arriving at the temple, he asks for the ‘gates of righteousness’ to open so he can enter and give thanks.
The priests answer: this is the Lord’s gate; only the righteous may enter. Jesus called himself the gate through which we enter.
Inside, he thanks God for answering him and becoming his salvation.
A stone rejected by the builders became the cornerstone. Jesus applied this to himself, rejected by the leaders yet made the foundation of God’s house. The Book of Mormon uses the same image.

f.w: The stone which the builders refused

f.g: The cornerstone or capstone that holds the building together.

n: This reversal is God’s doing, and it amazes us.

f.w: it is marvellous in our eyes

n: ‘This is the day the Lord has made’ — the day of his saving act. Christians sing it of Easter, the day of Christ’s Resurrection.

f.w: This is the day which the LORD hath made

n: ‘Save now, we pray!’ — in Hebrew, hoshiʿah-na, the source of ‘Hosanna.’ The crowds shouted this as Jesus entered Jerusalem.
‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD’ — sung by the crowds on Palm Sunday and quoted by Jesus about his return.

f.w: Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD

n: God has given us light. Bind the festival sacrifice with cords to the horns of the altar — perhaps leading a procession with branches up to the altar. Christ is the ultimate sacrifice.

f.g: Horn-shaped projections at the altar’s four corners.

n: A personal declaration: ‘You are my God; I will praise and exalt you.’
The psalm closes as it began — a frame of thanks for God’s goodness and enduring love.

f.w: O give thanks unto the LORD
